paragraphs: When data have symmetries, a useful network should respond consistently to those symmetries. Invariance means its output stays unchanged, while equivariance means its output changes in a corresponding way. Frame averaging approaches obtain these properties by averaging over selected transformations that depend on the input. The paper asks how to design those selections in a principled way.

The authors connect frames to canonicalization: mapping an input to a standard representative form. This connection provides a way to analyze how much work different frames require and to establish whether particular frames are optimal. It also reveals equivalences between methods that previously appeared different, giving a common explanation for their behavior.

Using this perspective, the authors construct new frames for eigenvectors. They report theoretical and empirical improvements over existing approaches, with some of the proposed frames achieving optimality. The contribution is therefore both a design principle and a concrete application: canonical forms help explain existing symmetry methods and guide the construction of better ones.
neurips-2024-a-canonicalization-perspect.tldr: Connecting frame averaging to canonical forms provides a principled way to compare symmetry methods and design improved frames.

paragraphs: Reducing the numerical precision of a language model's parameters can make deployment more efficient, but different parameters may tolerate that reduction differently. This paper finds that a small group of parameters has an unusually large influence on model performance. The authors call these influential values cherry parameters and observe this uneven distribution of importance across model families, sizes, and types.

CherryQ turns that observation into a quantization method. It identifies the influential parameters and keeps them at high precision, while assigning low precision much more aggressively to the remaining parameters. Its optimization handles these different precision levels together, making parameter importance central to how the model is compressed.

The reported experiments show improvements over existing quantization approaches in both perplexity and downstream tasks. In particular, the authors describe their 3-bit quantized Vicuna-1.5 models as competitive with their 16-bit counterparts. These results support selective precision allocation as a promising deployment strategy: retaining accuracy where parameters matter most can enable substantial compression elsewhere.
neurips-2024-cherry-on-top-parameter-het.tldr: CherryQ preserves a small set of influential parameters at high precision while quantizing the rest to improve language-model compression.

paragraphs: Binary statistical decision making uses evidence to choose between two possible states. The challenge is often to find the best decision strategy while respecting constraints. Both the desired objective and the restrictions can be expressed through integrals involving measurable functions, with the strategy itself appearing as one of the functions being optimized.

This paper develops a general formulation of that mathematical problem and characterizes its optimal solution in detail. Instead of treating each decision problem as an isolated derivation, the framework places many established and recently proposed formulations within one shared structure. The authors then demonstrate how the general characterization yields optimal strategies for these individual cases.

The value of the approach is its reusable mathematical machinery. When a binary decision problem fits the formulation, its solution can be derived through the common framework. This can simplify work on existing problems and help analyze new formulations relevant to machine learning. The stated contribution is a general account of optimal decision strategies, supported by derivations for diverse instances.
neurips-2024-constrained-binary-decision.tldr: A unified mathematical framework characterizes optimal strategies for a broad range of constrained binary decision problems.

paragraphs: Pretrained image networks represent pictures through internal features that capture useful visual information. Deep Degradation Response, or DDR, describes an image by measuring how those features change when the image undergoes degradation. The central idea is that an image's response to controlled damage can reveal properties that are useful for describing and assessing it.

The method supports flexible degradation controlled through text prompts, allowing the degradation process to adapt. Across extensive evaluations, the authors find strong correlations between DDR and image attributes including complexity, colorfulness, sharpness, and overall quality. These relationships suggest that feature changes under degradation can serve as a versatile image descriptor.

The paper also applies DDR to image assessment and restoration. It reports stronger blind image quality assessment than existing methods across multiple datasets, meaning quality can be assessed without a clean reference image. Used as an unsupervised training objective, DDR also improves deblurring and single-image super-resolution. The findings connect one descriptive signal to both evaluating images and guiding their restoration.
neurips-2024-ddr-exploiting-deep-degrada.tldr: DDR describes images through feature changes under controlled degradation, supporting image quality assessment and unsupervised restoration.

paragraphs: Real image noise can have structure and depend on the underlying signal, making it harder to remove than simple noise assumptions suggest. This paper combines a diffusion model's learned image prior with an adaptive description of the observed noise. The aim is to update the noise model while reconstructing the image during reverse diffusion.

The method uses a likelihood that treats noise components as independent but allows their distributions to differ. It places a prior on noise precision, the inverse of variance, and updates the precision posterior through variational Bayes during generation. A local Gaussian convolution further adjusts the estimated noise variance. Intermediate maximum a posteriori estimates balance this updated likelihood against the diffusion prior.

The final reconstruction results from propagating those intermediate estimates through the reverse process. The authors also investigate local priors within low-resolution diffusion models to handle high-resolution noisy images directly. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets support the method's effectiveness, indicating that adapting the noise description during reconstruction can make diffusion priors useful under more realistic noise conditions.
neurips-2024-diffusion-priors-for-variat.tldr: Adaptive noise estimation during reverse diffusion combines image priors and updated likelihoods to remove real-world image noise.

paragraphs: An agent exploring an unfamiliar environment can choose goals near the boundary of places it has already visited. However, a promising frontier goal may still be too difficult for its current policy to reach. Repeatedly choosing such goals can reduce useful exploration. This paper addresses that mismatch between where exploration would be valuable and where the agent can actually go.

Cluster Edge Exploration, abbreviated CE², groups states in a learned latent space according to how easily the current policy can move between them. It prioritizes accessible goals in sparsely explored regions. The agent first moves toward a cluster boundary with substantial exploration potential and then performs exploratory behavior from that location.

The authors evaluate the method on an ant robot navigating a maze, a robot arm manipulating objects on a cluttered table, and a robotic hand rotating objects. CE² explores more efficiently than the evaluated baselines and ablations. These results support making goal selection sensitive to current capabilities, so frontier exploration begins from states the agent is better positioned to reach.
neurips-2024-exploring-the-edges-of-late.tldr: CE² improves exploration by choosing promising cluster-boundary goals that remain accessible to the agent's current policy.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery requires learning about both familiar categories and new categories without explicit labels for all of them. Teacher-student methods can provide guidance in this setting, but the teacher lacks prior information about new classes. Its guidance can therefore become misaligned with what the student is learning, reducing the effectiveness of the training process.

The paper identifies inconsistent pattern learning as a central reason conventional teacher-student designs struggle here. Its proposed method, FlipClass, dynamically adjusts the teacher's attention using feedback from the student. This changes the relationship between the two models: the teacher's focus is updated to help them recognize patterns consistently across old and new categories.

Experiments across a range of benchmarks show that FlipClass significantly outperforms contemporary generalized category discovery methods. The findings support adapting the source of supervision as discovery proceeds. In a setting where the teacher has incomplete knowledge of the categories, synchronizing what teacher and student attend to can make their interaction more effective.
neurips-2024-flipped-classroom-aligning-.tldr: FlipClass improves generalized category discovery by updating the teacher's attention to align with the student's learning.

paragraphs: Being able to process a long input does not guarantee that a language model will use information throughout it effectively. Many models struggle to identify relevant material near the middle of their context. This paper targets that positional weakness through Multi-scale Positional Encoding, or Ms-PoE, which modifies how positions are represented without requiring fine-tuning or additional overhead.

Ms-PoE rescales position indices to reduce the long-distance decay associated with rotary positional encoding. It assigns different scaling ratios to different attention heads, creating a combination of short-distance and long-distance processing. The assignment is designed to preserve knowledge acquired during pretraining while improving access to information across the context.

Experiments with a broad range of language models support the approach. On Zero-SCROLLS, the authors report an average accuracy gain of up to 3.8 over the original models. The results suggest that adjusting positional encoding can improve how existing models use long inputs, with particular relevance to information that would otherwise be overlooked in the middle.
neurips-2024-found-in-the-middle-how-lan.tldr: Ms-PoE rescales positional information across attention heads to improve long-context use without fine-tuning or added overhead.

paragraphs: A world model lets a reinforcement learning agent reason about an environment when planning. This paper studies models written as Python code by a language model. Once generated, the code can be called during planning, offering the potential for more precise, reliable, interpretable, and efficient computation than repeatedly querying a language model.

Producing suitable code requires understanding the environment, implementing complicated logic correctly, and repairing a long program using feedback. The authors introduce Generate, Improve and Fix with Monte Carlo Tree Search, or GIF-MCTS, to address these demands. They also create the Code World Models Benchmark, containing 18 reinforcement learning environments with textual descriptions and curated trajectories for offline evaluation.

GIF-MCTS outperforms all evaluated baselines on that benchmark and two additional benchmarks. The authors further demonstrate that its generated world models can support planning, producing agents with greatly improved sample efficiency and inference speed. These findings connect code-generation quality to the practical usefulness of the resulting programs within model-based reinforcement learning.
neurips-2024-generating-code-world-model.tldr: GIF-MCTS guides language models in generating and repairing executable world models that improve reinforcement learning planning.

paragraphs: Language models can retain substantial factual knowledge, but the process by which pretraining builds and preserves that knowledge is less understood. This paper examines factual learning as a changing process during training. It considers both the acquisition of facts and the forgetting that can follow as the model continues to encounter training data.

The authors observe that pretraining on more data does not significantly improve the studied ability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. They find forgetting in both memorization and generalization, with faster forgetting in models trained on duplicated data. Larger training batches, by contrast, can improve robustness to forgetting in their observations.

Their interpretation is that exposure gradually raises the probability assigned to factual information, while subsequent training dilutes those gains through forgetting. This account offers plausible explanations for weak performance on long-tail knowledge and for benefits from deduplicating pretraining data. The findings frame factual knowledge as a balance between repeated learning gains and later losses, rather than a simple consequence of accumulating more training data.
neurips-2024-how-do-large-language-model.tldr: The study describes factual learning during pretraining as incremental acquisition offset by forgetting, with data duplication and batch size affecting retention.

paragraphs: Choosing a language-model architecture involves trade-offs among predictive performance, latency, energy consumption, and GPU memory. Measuring every candidate on multiple devices would require substantial training and evaluation work. HW-GPT-Bench provides a way to explore these choices through predictions of hardware behavior for GPT-2-family architectures containing up to 1.55 billion parameters.

The benchmark uses surrogate models to approximate hardware metrics across 13 devices. Their calibrated predictions include uncertainty estimates and account for measurement noise whose magnitude varies, particularly in latency and energy measurements. To estimate perplexity, the benchmark uses weight sharing from neural architecture search, drawing pretrained weights from the largest GPT-2 model.

The authors demonstrate that the benchmark can simulate the progress of several multi-objective optimization algorithms within seconds. This makes it useful for studying how architecture search balances competing requirements under hardware constraints. Its contribution is a fast evaluation framework grounded in predicted hardware behavior and shared model weights, enabling broader exploration without exhaustively training and measuring every candidate.
neurips-2024-hw-gpt-bench-hardware-aware.tldr: HW-GPT-Bench combines hardware surrogates and shared weights to rapidly study language-model architecture trade-offs across 13 devices.

paragraphs: A signed distance function represents a surface through distances whose signs distinguish its two sides. Estimating one from noisy point measurements is useful for reconstruction and denoising. The paper addresses a trade-off between data-driven methods that can generalize poorly and methods fitted to individual point clouds that can converge slowly, especially under heavy noise.

The proposed approach starts from a data-driven prior and fine-tunes it to a single noisy point cloud. A statistical reasoning algorithm operating in local regions makes this adaptation possible without signed-distance supervision, a clean point cloud, or point normals. The prior supplies a useful initialization, helping the subsequent fitting process converge much faster.

Numerical and visual comparisons on widely used shape and scene benchmarks show advantages over the compared state-of-the-art methods in surface reconstruction and point-cloud denoising. The approach combines knowledge learned from data with adjustment to the particular observed object or scene. Its reported benefits include better generalization, faster inference, and greater accuracy in learning neural signed distance functions.
neurips-2024-inferring-neural-signed-dis.tldr: Fine-tuning learned priors through local statistical reasoning improves signed-distance estimation from a single noisy point cloud.

paragraphs: Distributed training divides gradient computation among workers and combines their results at a parameter server. Some workers run slowly or fail, so gradient coding assigns redundant work that allows the server to reconstruct the gradient despite missing contributions. Many existing protocols treat workers as either finished or failed, discarding useful partial work from slower workers.

This paper introduces coding protocols that incorporate those partial contributions. The authors describe the protocols as computationally efficient, communication efficient, and numerically stable. They also study the order in which each worker processes its assigned data chunks. For an important class of assignments, they provide efficient algorithms for optimizing that order because it affects total execution time.

For exact gradient reconstruction, the proposed protocol is reported to run around twice as fast as the original class of protocols. For approximate reconstruction, the reconstructed gradient has mean-squared error several orders of magnitude lower. The findings show how retaining partial progress can improve either recovery speed or approximation quality, depending on the reconstruction objective.
neurips-2024-leveraging-partial-straggle.tldr: New gradient coding protocols use slow workers' partial results to accelerate exact recovery and improve approximate gradient accuracy.

paragraphs: Approximate matrix multiplication aims to reduce computation while accepting some numerical error. Its appeal has grown alongside the resource demands of large language models, but choosing an effective approach requires understanding more than the algorithm alone. This paper examines how algorithm design, implementation behavior, dataset properties, and application requirements jointly influence the result.

Through testing across diverse datasets and scenarios, the authors find that algorithm selection substantially affects the trade-off between efficiency and accuracy. Memory access is an especially consequential operational factor. Dataset characteristics also matter for whether an approximation method succeeds in an application, supporting choices tailored to the data and computational setting.

The paper introduces LibAMM, a toolkit containing a broad collection of approximate multiplication algorithms, benchmarks, and experiment-management tools. It provides infrastructure for investigating these choices and applying the methods in practice. The central finding is that effective approximate multiplication depends on matching strategies to context; its practical contribution is a shared toolkit for making that matching process easier to study.
neurips-2024-libamm-empirical-insights-i.tldr: LibAMM studies how algorithms, memory access, and datasets shape approximate matrix multiplication's efficiency–accuracy trade-offs.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision encoders can memorize individual images even when trained on millions of examples. This paper investigates where that memorization occurs inside the network. It introduces LayerMem and UnitMem to measure memorization at the level of whole layers and individual units, without labels or a specified downstream task and using a forward pass.

The authors examine convolutional and transformer encoders trained with different datasets and self-supervised frameworks. They find that memorization increases with depth, while strongly memorizing units occur throughout the network. A substantial fraction of units shows high memorization of individual examples, contrasting with supervised models. Atypical examples produce much stronger memorization than standard examples.

For vision transformers, most memorization is found in fully connected layers. Together, these observations separate a broad depth trend from the locations of particular memorizing units. The authors also show that localization has potential to improve fine-tuning and guide pruning. The contribution makes memorization more spatially specific within an encoder, which can help inform decisions about how the model is adapted or reduced.
neurips-2024-localizing-memorization-in-.tldr: LayerMem and UnitMem locate memorization inside self-supervised vision encoders, revealing patterns relevant to fine-tuning and pruning.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential multiclass prediction in a transductive setting when the number of possible labels can be unbounded. Earlier techniques for finite label sets did not extend to this case. The authors introduce the Level-constrained Littlestone dimension, a measure of a prediction class's combinatorial complexity, and show that it characterizes online learnability in this setting.

In the realizable case, they prove that the best achievable worst-case expected mistake count has only three possible growth patterns over T rounds: linear in T, logarithmic in T, or constant. A second measure, the Level-constrained Branching dimension, characterizes constant mistake bounds through its finiteness. Together, the two dimensions determine which growth regime applies.

The work also constructs learning algorithms whose upper bounds avoid dependence on the label-set size, improving existing multiclass bounds and accommodating extremely large or unbounded sets. A new sequential notion of shattering is central to the construction. Finally, the authors establish expected regret bounds in the agnostic setting, extending the analysis beyond realizable prediction.
neurips-2024-multiclass-transductive-onl.tldr: New combinatorial dimensions characterize transductive online learnability and mistake-rate regimes even with unbounded label sets.

paragraphs: Many statistical tasks require a distribution conditioned on available information, rather than a single predicted value. Neural Conditional Probability, or NCP, learns conditional distributions through an operator-theoretic approach. From that representation, it can construct conditional confidence regions and obtain statistics including quantiles, means, and covariances, supporting several forms of uncertainty analysis.

NCP uses one unconditional training phase and then supports efficient inference as the conditioning changes, without retraining. Neural networks supply the approximation capacity needed to handle varied and complex distributions. This separation between training and changing inference conditions is central to the method's usefulness across different statistical queries.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for optimization consistency and statistical accuracy. In experiments, an NCP model with two hidden layers matches or outperforms leading methods. These results show that a relatively small architecture, paired with a theoretically motivated loss, can be competitive with more complex alternatives in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines reusable conditional inference with both mathematical analysis and empirical evidence.
neurips-2024-neural-conditional-probabil.tldr: NCP learns conditional distributions in one training phase, enabling changing statistical queries without retraining.

paragraphs: In online prediction, a learner answers each arriving instance before seeing its correct label. A rule is consistent when its fraction of mistakes eventually tends to zero. This paper studies that property for nearest-neighbor prediction in the realizable setting, where the answers follow an underlying target function. The question is when this simple rule can keep improving along a stream of instances.

Earlier consistency results required strong conditions, such as independent, identically distributed instances or well-separated label classes. The authors prove consistency for every measurable target function in doubling metric spaces under a different assumption on the instance-generating process. That process must be uniformly absolutely continuous relative to a finite, upper doubling measure.

The result broadens the theoretical conditions under which nearest-neighbor prediction is known to work online. Its guarantee concerns the long-run mistake rate, so it does not require mistakes to cease after a finite time. The geometric and process assumptions remain part of the theorem: within those conditions, consistency holds across all measurable target functions.
neurips-2024-online-consistency-of-the-n.tldr: Nearest-neighbor prediction has vanishing online mistake rates under specified geometric and process assumptions beyond earlier consistency settings.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with unfamiliar agents must adapt to behavior it has not encountered before. Many opponent-modeling methods address this by predicting the other agent's next actions. This paper argues that such a short-term focus can restrict adaptation in complex tasks, where understanding what the other agent is trying to accomplish may be more useful.

The proposed approach infers an opponent's subgoals from historical trajectories. Different policies may pursue the same intermediate objective through different actions, so subgoals can provide a common representation across unfamiliar opponents. The method includes two subgoal-selection modes, one for cooperative games and another for general-sum games, reflecting different relationships between the agents' objectives.

Across a variety of tasks, the authors report more effective adaptation than existing methods. The rationale is that shared subgoals can support generalization even when the precise action policy changes. The empirical findings support this approach in the evaluated tasks, linking higher-level behavioral inference to improved adaptation without requiring identical behavior across opponents.
neurips-2024-opponent-modeling-based-on-.tldr: Inferring opponents' subgoals from past trajectories improves adaptation to unfamiliar agents in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses judgments about preferred behavior to guide an agent. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is a case where those judgments come from people. Many approaches optimize average reward, but applications that need risk awareness require attention to the distribution of outcomes. The paper addresses this need in a one-episode-reward setting.

The authors establish that two quantile-based risk objectives, called nested and static objectives, are applicable to preference-based learning. They introduce RA-PbRL, an algorithm designed to optimize either form. This provides a route to incorporating risk preferences into a setting where conventional risk-sensitive objectives are described as inapplicable.

The theoretical analysis gives regret upper bounds that grow sublinearly with the number of episodes. Such bounds mean that the upper bound on regret per episode decreases as experience accumulates. Empirical results also support the findings. The contribution connects risk-aware objectives, an optimization algorithm, and learning guarantees, extending preference-based reinforcement learning beyond an exclusive focus on mean reward.
neurips-2024-ra-pbrl-provably-efficient-.tldr: RA-PbRL optimizes quantile-based risk objectives from preferences and has sublinear regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Text embeddings represent text in a form useful for retrieval, clustering, and assessing semantic similarity. This paper studies how to produce embedding models from pretrained decoder-only language models while using a given computational budget effectively. The relevant choices include the starting model's size, the amount of training data, and the method used for fine-tuning.

The authors develop an algorithm that produces compute-optimal configurations across those choices for contrastive training. Extensive experiments provide the resulting recipe at different budget levels. Considering these decisions together matters because a budget must cover both the selected model and the work required to adapt it into an embedding model.

The findings suggest that full fine-tuning produces optimal models at lower computational budgets, while Low-Rank Adaptation produces optimal models at higher budgets. This makes the preferred fine-tuning method dependent on the available compute in the studied setting. The practical contribution is guidance for choosing a complete training configuration, rather than selecting model size, data quantity, and adaptation method independently.
neurips-2024-repurposing-language-models.tldr: An empirical recipe jointly selects model size, data quantity, and fine-tuning method for compute-efficient text embedding training.

paragraphs: Empirical scaling laws often show that increasing model size and training data steadily reduces test error. That pattern seems difficult to reconcile with the usual expectation that larger models increase variance error. This paper investigates the tension in an infinite-dimensional linear regression setting, using a model with M parameters trained on N examples through one-pass stochastic gradient descent.

The analysis assumes a Gaussian prior for the optimal parameter and a data covariance spectrum that follows a power law with exponent a greater than one. Under these assumptions, the reducible test error scales as Θ(M^{−(a−1)} + N^{−(a−1)/a}). Both terms decrease as their corresponding resources increase, with rates determined by the spectrum's exponent.

Variance still increases with model size in the analysis, but the implicit regularization of stochastic gradient descent makes other error terms dominate it. It therefore does not appear in the resulting scaling bound. Numerical simulations support the theory. The result provides a mathematical explanation consistent with empirical neural scaling laws within this specified linear-regression model.
neurips-2024-scaling-laws-in-linear-regr.tldr: Under specified linear-regression assumptions, SGD's implicit regularization yields scaling laws where increasing model size and data reduces reducible error.

paragraphs: Graphs describe entities and the relationships connecting them. Many text-attributed graph datasets attach rich language descriptions to entities but describe relationships only through binary connections or category labels. This makes it difficult to study the contextual meaning of connections. TEG-DB addresses that gap by including substantial textual descriptions on both nodes and edges.

The collection contains large-scale datasets spanning domains such as citation and social networks. Alongside the datasets, the authors benchmark pretrained language models, graph neural networks, and combinations of the two. These experiments assess how well current techniques can use the language associated with both entities and their relationships.

The contribution is shared data and an evaluation setting for studying richer graph representations. Describing an edge in language gives methods additional relationship information to work with, while the benchmark makes their use of that information an explicit research question. The project aims to encourage methods that exploit both kinds of descriptions for improved graph analysis and deeper understanding of real-world networks.
neurips-2024-teg-db-a-comprehensive-data.tldr: TEG-DB provides datasets and benchmarks for graphs with rich textual descriptions of both entities and relationships.

paragraphs: Language models can produce harmful, biased, or toxic content when prompts bypass their safeguards. This paper introduces Tree of Attacks with Pruning, or TAP, an automated method for finding such jailbreaks using only black-box access to the target model. The method therefore studies vulnerabilities through interaction with the model rather than access to its internal parameters.

TAP uses an attacker language model to iteratively revise candidate prompts. Before submitting candidates to the target, it evaluates them and removes those considered unlikely to succeed. This pruning reduces the number of target queries, making the search more efficient while retaining promising candidates for further refinement.

In the reported evaluations, TAP achieves jailbreaks for more than 80% of the tested prompts against models including GPT4-Turbo and GPT4o. It improves on previous leading black-box methods while using fewer queries, and it also succeeds against models protected by guardrails such as LlamaGuard. These empirical results demonstrate that automated prompt search can expose substantial weaknesses in the evaluated safeguards.
neurips-2024-tree-of-attacks-jailbreakin.tldr: TAP uses iterative prompt refinement and pruning to find black-box jailbreaks with high empirical success and fewer target queries.

paragraphs: Text-guided 3D generation can produce appealing assets, but words and available reference images can restrict the shapes users express. YouDream adds explicit anatomical control for animal generation through a 3D pose prior. Two-dimensional views of that pose control a text-to-image diffusion model, connecting a specified body structure to the generation process.

The authors report that this approach can create novel imaginary animals beyond the capabilities of previous text-to-3D methods. It can also preserve anatomical consistency, a difficulty for earlier approaches. The pose prior supplies a structural basis for the desired animal while diffusion guidance contributes to the generated asset's visual appearance.

For commonly observed animals, the paper introduces a fully automated pipeline. A multi-agent language-model system adapts poses from a limited library of animal poses, avoiding the need for a person to construct the 3D pose. A user study finds a preference for YouDream's generated animals over the compared alternatives. The work combines controllable generation with automation for more familiar animal forms.
neurips-2024-youdream-generating-anatomi.tldr: YouDream uses 3D pose guidance to generate anatomically controllable animals and automates pose adaptation for common animals.
